title: SWIFT vs ACH vs wire: how SWIFT payments work for business
summary: What SWIFT is, how a SWIFT payment works, and when a finance team should use SWIFT, ACH or a domestic wire to pay a supplier.
body_markdown:
When a finance team needs to pay an overseas supplier, the bank or payment provider often offers more than one rail: ACH, a domestic wire, or a SWIFT payment. The names get used as if they were the same thing, and they are not. SWIFT is a messaging network banks use to instruct cross-border payments, ACH is a U.S. domestic clearing system, and a domestic U.S. wire usually travels on a rail such as Fedwire. Choosing the wrong one can add days, correspondent fees, or a returned payment.


## The key points


- SWIFT (the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication) carries payment instructions between banks; it does not itself move the underlying funds.
- ACH is a U.S. domestic clearing system, so ACH alone is not the rail you use to pay a supplier in another country.
- A domestic wire, such as a payment on the Fedwire Funds Service, moves money between U.S. banks and usually costs more than ACH.
- The time a SWIFT transfer takes depends on cut-off times, currency, compliance checks and the number of correspondent banks, so it helps to plan in business days.
- Jeeves Pay lets a finance team pay suppliers in more than 150 countries in up to 40 currencies from one payment form.


## What is SWIFT in banking, and how do SWIFT payments work?


SWIFT is a messaging network that banks and other financial institutions use to send payment instructions to one another. The Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication runs the network; it is not a settlement system and it is not the money itself. (This article is about SWIFT in banking, not the Swift programming language.)


A typical SWIFT payment for a business follows four steps:


1. Your accounts payable team instructs its bank or payment provider to pay a supplier abroad.
2. Your bank sends a SWIFT message with the payment instruction toward the supplier's bank.
3. If the two banks do not hold accounts with each other, one or more correspondent banks sit in the middle and pass the payment along.
4. The beneficiary bank credits the supplier's account.


Because SWIFT only carries the instruction, the funds settle through the accounts banks hold with one another. That is why a SWIFT cross-border payment can touch several banks, and why each one can affect the timing and the final amount. You can read SWIFT's own description of the network on[swift.com](https://www.swift.com/about-us) .


## What is a SWIFT/BIC code, and what is SWIFT gpi?


### What is a SWIFT/BIC code?


A SWIFT code, also called a BIC (Business Identifier Code), identifies a bank on the SWIFT network. It is usually 8 or 11 characters long. A SWIFT/BIC code is not an account number and it is not an IBAN: it tells the network which bank to reach, while the account number or IBAN tells that bank which account to credit.


### What is SWIFT gpi?


SWIFT gpi (global payments innovation) is an industry improvement from SWIFT that lets participating banks track a cross-border payment as it moves between banks. Whether you can see that tracking depends on your bank or provider; it is an industry capability, not something every payment includes.


## SWIFT vs ACH: what's the difference for a business?


The short answer: ACH is a U.S. domestic clearing system, and SWIFT is the network banks use to instruct cross-border payments. For a domestic U.S. vendor, ACH is usually the everyday rail. For a supplier in another country, ACH by itself is usually not the right rail.


The Automated Clearing House network processes batches of electronic payments between U.S. bank accounts, such as payroll, vendor payments and direct debits. The Federal Reserve operates one of the ACH operators, FedACH, and describes the service on its[FedACH overview](https://www.federalreserve.gov/paymentsystems/fedach_about.htm) . ACH payments are typically lower cost, and they settle on a batch schedule rather than one by one.


## How does a SWIFT payment differ from ACH?


ACH is a U.S. domestic clearing system, and SWIFT is the network banks use to instruct cross-border payments. A SWIFT payment works differently. Your bank sends an individual instruction over the SWIFT network to a bank in another country, sometimes through correspondent banks. That flexibility is what lets you pay a supplier in Europe or Asia, but it also adds steps and possible fees.

## ACH vs wire vs SWIFT: when should a business use each one?


Use ACH for ordinary domestic U.S. payments, a domestic wire when a U.S. payment needs to arrive faster, and SWIFT when you need to pay a business in another country. Each rail fits a different job.


- **ACH.** It works well for payroll, recurring domestic vendors and payments where same-day arrival is not essential. It is usually the lowest-cost option for U.S. accounts payable.
- **Domestic wire.** A domestic wire moves funds between U.S. banks one payment at a time, often on the[Fedwire Funds Service](https://www.federalreserve.gov/paymentsystems/fedfunds_about.htm) . It is typically used for urgent or high-value domestic payments and usually costs more than ACH.
- **SWIFT.** A SWIFT payment fits international supplier payments, when the beneficiary bank needs to be reached over the international messaging network.


## Is an international wire the same as a SWIFT payment?


The most common confusion is the "international wire." Many banks label an overseas payment a wire, and that payment is often instructed over SWIFT. So when a supplier abroad asks for "a wire," they usually mean a SWIFT cross-border payment, not a domestic Fedwire transfer. It helps to ask the supplier for their SWIFT/BIC code and account details up front, so your accounts payable team picks the right rail the first time.


A SWIFT payment fits international supplier payments, when the beneficiary bank needs to be reached over the international messaging network.


## How long does a SWIFT transfer take internationally?


A SWIFT transfer has no single universal delivery time. The timing of an international SWIFT payment depends on several factors, so it is safer to plan in business days than to expect same-day arrival.


The main factors that affect how long a SWIFT transfer takes are:


- **Cut-off times.** A payment sent after your bank's daily cut-off usually starts the next business day.
- **Correspondent banks.** Each intermediary bank between your bank and the supplier's bank adds a step.
- **Currency and time zones.** Currency conversion and banking hours in the destination country can add time.
- **Compliance checks.** Sanctions and anti-money-laundering reviews can hold a payment until a bank clears it.
- **Data quality.** A missing or incorrect field can delay the payment or send it back.


Tracking helps finance teams set expectations. Banks that participate in SWIFT gpi can show where a payment is in the chain, but availability depends on your bank or provider. We recommend confirming the expected range for each corridor with your bank or payment provider and sharing it with the supplier, so nobody treats a single number as a guarantee.


## What information do you need to send a SWIFT payment?


To send a SWIFT payment, you need the supplier's bank details and payment details, collected before the first payment. A missing or swapped field is one of the most common reasons a cross-border payment is delayed or returned.


A typical beneficiary record for a SWIFT payment includes:


- The beneficiary's legal name, exactly as it appears on the bank account.
- The account number, or the IBAN in countries that use IBAN.
- The beneficiary bank's SWIFT/BIC code.
- The beneficiary's address, if the bank or corridor requires it.
- The currency and the amount.
- A purpose or memo, such as the invoice number.
- Any intermediary bank details the supplier provides.


It helps to confirm new or changed bank details with the supplier through a separate, trusted channel before you pay. Changed bank details are a common route for payment fraud, and a short verification call can prevent a costly mistake. Once the record is correct, store it so your accounts payable team does not retype it for every invoice.

## Frequently asked questions


### What is the difference between a SWIFT code and an IBAN?


A SWIFT/BIC code identifies the bank, while an IBAN identifies the individual account in countries that use the IBAN standard. The United States does not use IBANs. A U.S. beneficiary usually provides a routing number and an account number, plus a SWIFT/BIC code when the payment comes from abroad. Many international payments need both a bank code and an account identifier.


### Can I use ACH to pay an overseas supplier?


Usually not by itself. ACH is a U.S. domestic clearing system for payments between U.S. bank accounts. Paying a supplier in another country typically requires a cross-border rail, often instructed over the SWIFT network and commonly labelled an international wire. We recommend confirming the available options with your bank or payment provider before you set up the supplier.


### Who pays SWIFT fees?


SWIFT fees can be charged by the sending bank, by correspondent banks along the route, and sometimes by the beneficiary bank. Who bears them depends on the charge option chosen when the payment is sent and on the corridor. There is no single public fee.


### How can a business pay international suppliers with Jeeves Pay?

The exchange rate and the converted amount appear before you send, and a proof-of-payment PDF can be shared with the supplier. ### Is SWIFT the same as a wire transfer?


Not exactly. In the United States, a wire often means a domestic payment between U.S. banks, for example on the Fedwire Funds Service. An international wire is usually a payment instructed over the SWIFT network. SWIFT carries the instruction between banks in different countries; the domestic wire moves funds between banks inside one country.


Choosing between SWIFT, ACH and a wire comes down to where the supplier banks and how quickly the payment needs to arrive. With the right rail and a clean beneficiary record, your finance team can pay suppliers abroad with fewer surprises.
